references.text: Moses intercedes for Pharaoh, just as he did earlier during the plague of frogs, and promises to pray to the Lord on his behalf.
Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to the Lord, and the plague stops—the same pattern seen here with the plague of flies.
Moses departs from Pharaoh and prays to the Lord, who removes the plague of locusts—a parallel intercession pattern.
Pharaoh hardened his heart and deceived Moses earlier, something Moses warns will happen again.
Direct fulfillment of Moses' warning—Pharaoh hardened his heart once more and refused to let the people go.
Abraham intercedes and prays for Abimelech, an early example of intercession in the books of Moses.
Job is asked to pray for his friends, a similar intercessory role that Moses holds here.
King Hezekiah asks the prophet Isaiah to intercede, parallel to Pharaoh's request to Moses.
Paul warns against deceiving God, reflecting Moses' warning to Pharaoh not to continue deceiving.
Both verses illustrate Pharaoh's repeated tactic of offering compromises regarding sacrifice to avoid full liberation.
Contrast between Pharaoh's deceitful compromises in verse 25 and his forced complete expulsion in verse 8.
Both verses reveal Pharaoh's strategy of compromise: in verse 7 he limits the departure, while in verse 25 Moses warns that he will refuse sacrifice.
The prophecy of complete expulsion in verse 8 explains the context for Moses' fear of deception in verse 25.
